groups.text: java C and kotlinc don't produce machine code.
They produce bytecode: small instructions for the J V M, which HotSpot turns into machine code while the program runs.
This is the loop body of settle, which adds up a batch of payments.
Bytecode twenty is the call to feeCents.
Bytecode thirty-one tests for a refund.
Nothing is compiled at first.
Every method starts in the interpreter, a loop inside the J V M that reads one bytecode instruction at a time and carries it out.
Meanwhile the J V M counts the calls, and the jumps back to the top of each loop.
At about two hundred, a compiler thread compiles the method with C one, in the background.
C one is quick, and optimizes a little.
Its code also records a profile: which way each branch went, and which receiver types reached each call.
About five thousand calls later, C two compiles it again, slowly and hard, from that profile.
The J V M raises these thresholds when the compile queues are long, so treat them as orders of magnitude.
C two bets on the profile.
Every receiver was a Card, so it inlines Card's feeCents behind a cheap class check.
The refund branch never ran, so C two leaves it out, and puts an uncommon trap there.
Then a refund arrives.
The trap fires, and the J V M deoptimizes.
It rebuilds an interpreter frame from the compiled one, and carries on there.
The C two code is made not entrant.
The method profiles again, now with refunds, and gets compiled again.
A burst of this after a deploy is normal.
A steady stream, hours after startup, is worth a look.
